title: Slab Coordinator + KV Coalescer: attention kernel design notes
content:
Summary:
This note captures an experimental design for a slab-based KV allocator and an upstream "coalescer"/coordinator that steers DMA-prefetches and small fused-attention kernels. Goal is to reduce per-token latency variance and memory fragmentation for long-context workloads with paged KV while preserving high occupancy for Flash-style attention kernels.

Motivation / problem statement:
- Paged-KV workloads cause high fragmentation: many small, short-lived KV slabs interleave with large persistent context (chat histories) leading to wasted device memory and reduced ability to batch tokens.
- Naive prefetch (per-request or per-token) creates many small DMA ops, hurting PCIe/NVLink efficiency and causing kernel launch jitter.
- Kernel fusion (attn + KV hydrate + dehydrate) needs predictable placements for KV so fused paths can assume contiguous regions; fragmentation breaks fusion and forces slower code paths.
- Need to maintain low tail latency for 95/99th percentiles for interactive workloads while also maximizing throughput for batch/backfill.

Design goals / constraints:
- Keep memory layout friendly for fused kernels: prefer contiguous slabs that can be referenced by a compact (pointer+len) descriptor.
- Coalesce small KV allocations into shared slabs when safe (tenant isolation and eviction semantics respected).
- Use asynchronous DMA + CUDA streams to prefetch and overlap compute, but avoid creating dozens of small streams/ops per token.
- Provide a coordinator that can merge prefetch requests across in-flight microbatches and decide between immediate DMA vs. lazy hydration.
- Maintain observable metrics and cheap heuristics so Product/Console can show quality vs. cost tradeoffs.

High-level approach:
1) Slab allocator: allocate device memory in slab sizes (configurable; e.g., 256KB / 1MB / 4MB classes). New small KV segments are appended into an active slab for that class. Slabs are per-tenant or per-model-group for isolation.
2) Descriptor table: each logical KV entry maps to (slab-id, offset, length, version) recorded in a device-resident descriptor array + mirrored host metadata for eviction decisions. Descriptor entries are compact (64-bit for pointer+12-bit for len + version).
3) KV Coalescer / Slab Coordinator: a lightweight on-device/host component that converts many small hydrate requests into fewer coalesced DMA ranges. It maintains a prefetch queue keyed by slab id and target offsets; adjacent offsets are merged up to a configurable merge-window (e.g., 64KB).
4) Stream mapping: we maintain N CUDA streams per GPU (N small, e.g., 2–4) dedicated to prefetching and 1 high-priority stream for fused-attn compute. Prefetches are scheduled onto prefetch streams with batched cuMemcpyAsync calls for merged ranges.
5) Kernel fusion hints: fused-attn kernels will be compiled with a slab-descriptor fast-path: if KV segments for all kv-ids in batch are contiguous and resident, run fused path; else fallback to generic flash/attention path that does dynamic gather.

Key data structures / APIs:
- SlabHdr { slab_id, base_ptr, size, free_offset, tenant_id, last_touch_ts } (host-managed)
- KVDescriptor[n] (device array) indexable by token-cohort id -> (slab_id, offset, len, version)
- PrefetchRequest { slab_id, start_off, end_off, priority, request_id }
- Coordinator API (host): submit_prefetchs(list<Request>), drain_prefetchs(), promote_slab_to_fused(slab_id)

Coalescing heuristics:
- Merge contiguous requests when gap <= MERGE_GAP (default 4KB).
- Prefer merging across requests within a small time-window W (default 1–2ms).
- Bounded growth: cap coalesced range to MAX_COALESCE (e.g., 256KB) to avoid dragging large unrelated ranges into memory.
- Priority: interactive requests (low latency) tagged high priority -> prefer small, earlier DMA complete; background batch requests can be coalesced aggressively.
- Tenant isolation: coalescing allowed only within same tenant/model-group. Cross-tenant coalescing disabled.

Eviction & compaction strategy:
- Slab LRU at slab granularity; when free space insufficient, evict oldest slab(s) in tenant's pool.
- For fragmentation heavy tenants, background compaction can be run: allocate a new slab, migrate live segments (batched copy), update descriptors atomically, then free old slab. Background compaction uses low-priority streams.
- Eviction should ensure version bump so in-flight kernels detect stale descriptors and fall back to safe path. We add a per-descriptor version; kernels check it at hydrate time and signal fallback if mismatch.

Scheduling / admission control:
- Coordinator groups incoming requests by sequence length bucket and slab locality. If a request misses and would trigger many small DMAs, it can either: (a) block briefly to allow coalescing window, (b) route to quantized/fallback kernel that hydrates on-demand, or (c) issue priority small DMA.
- Admission uses token-priority aging: very short interactive sequences get priority to avoid tail latency spikes; long generation streams get lower prefetch priority and are aggregated.

Kernel integration points:
- Fused-attn kernel expects: per-batch slab descriptors in contiguous descriptor buffer. If check passes, run fused-attn+KV load path with direct pointer loads.
- Otherwise, run fallback flash-attention kernel that calls a small gather utility to fetch KV from possibly non-contiguous device memory.
- Provide a micro-kernel for in-place hydration that accepts a coalesced range and performs vectorized copy + alignment for cache-line friendly reads for subsequent attention calls.

Concurrency and correctness notes:
- Atomic descriptor updates: update descriptor version high->low with fence to ensure kernels either see old consistent state or new consistent state.
- Kernel-side checks: early check of descriptor versions before heavy compute; if mismatch detected, early abort and requeue on safe stream. This avoids wasted compute work.

Metrics to observe:
- slab fragmentation (bytes free but unusable), slab occupancy per tenant, descriptor re-writes per second
- number of prefetch DMAs per second; mean coalesced range size
- flash-fused-path hit rate (percentage of attention batches that took fused fast path)
- latency p50/p95/p99 for interactive and batch workloads separately
- GPU utilization and stream stalls attributed to small DMAs

Microbench plan (initial):
- Synthetic: 1) many tiny segments (32B–512B) random insertion; 2) long chat streams w/ periodic short contexts to verify slab thrash. Measure fragmentation and fused-path hit rate.
- End-to-end: run chatbench with 2k/4k contexts, 30 concurrent users, compare: no-slab baseline vs slab-coalescer with MERGE_GAP=4KB and MAX_COALESCE=256KB. Track p95 latency and tokens/sec.

Expected tradeoffs / risks:
- Background compaction cost vs. memory win: compaction requires extra device-to-device copies (or host roundtrip) and can briefly increase memory usage. Need conservative triggers.
- Complexity of descriptor versioning and kernel abort handling risks subtle races. Keep checks simple and observable.
- Over-coalescing can bring in large, unnecessary memory ranges causing eviction churn. Use conservative MAX_COALESCE defaults.

Implementation milestones / TODOs:
- [ ] Prototype slab allocator (host-side metadata + device descriptor array) — Rafael
- [ ] Implement coalescer queue + merge window logic — Maya
- [ ] Small-number CUDA streams mapping tests and cuMemcpyAsync batching — Liu
- [ ] Integrate fused-kernel fast-path checks (descriptor contiguous/resident) — Ava
- [ ] Bench harness (chatbench + synthetic) and metrics export to Console — eng-dex

Open questions for next sync:
- How aggressive should compaction be for multi-tenant hosts? cost model?
- Do we expose coalesce parameters to user/console or keep internal auto-tuning?
- Fallback latency budget: how long can we hold a request to allow coalescing without violating SLOs?

Notes / references:
- See GH PR: runtime/pull/482 for initial descriptor layout prototype
- Related Slack: slab-kv-prefetch thread (links above)
- Jira RUNTIME-743: slab allocator design epic

Short-term experiment we can run now:
- Build host-side slab allocator + simple coalescer that groups requests within 1ms window and merges gaps <=4KB. Run synthetic microbench with many small KV entries and measure DMA ops/sec and fused-path hit rate.

If this looks good, next step is to spin a small prototype that keeps all logic host-side (no on-device coordinator) to validate heuristics before moving latency-sensitive checks into kernels.
